proof_nl:
Write an alternating permutation of length r as a permutation c_1,...,c_r with c_1 < c_2 > c_3 < c_4 > ... . First note that the number of reverse-alternating permutations c_1 > c_2 < c_3 > ... of {1,...,r} is also E_r, by the bijection c_i -> r+1-c_i.

For odd j, the number of alternating permutations of {1,...,n} with 1 in position j is exactly w_j. Indeed, in any alternating permutation the odd positions are valleys, so the minimum 1 can occur only at an odd position. Fix such a j. Choose the j-1 values lying to the left of 1; there are binom(n-1,j-1) choices. After order-preserving relabelling, the left block becomes an alternating permutation of length j-1, so there are E_{j-1} possibilities. The right block starts with a descent, hence is reverse-alternating; after complementing its values it becomes alternating, so there are E_{n-j} possibilities. Conversely these data reconstruct the original permutation uniquely. Therefore the count is binom(n-1,j-1) E_{j-1} E_{n-j} = w_j.

Similarly, for even j, the number of alternating permutations of {1,...,n} with n in position j is also w_j. Indeed, in an alternating permutation the even positions are peaks, so the maximum n can occur only at an even position. Fix such a j. Choose the j-1 values lying to the left of n; there are binom(n-1,j-1) choices. After standardization, both the left block and the right block are alternating permutations of lengths j-1 and n-j, so the count is again binom(n-1,j-1) E_{j-1} E_{n-j} = w_j.

Summing over all odd positions of 1 gives S_odd = E_n, and summing over all even positions of n gives S_even = E_n. So in fact S_odd = S_even = E_n for every n.

Now set F(x) = sum_{r>=0} E_r x^r/r!, and W_n(z) = sum_{j=1}^n w_j z^{j-1}. From the previous paragraph, with m = n-1, we get
2 E_{m+1} = sum_{k=0}^m binom(m,k) E_k E_{m-k}.
Therefore 2 F'(x) = 1 + F(x)^2.

Let G(x) = sec x + tan x. A direct calculation gives 2 G'(x) = 1 + G(x)^2 and G(0)=1. For a power series H(x)=1+h_1 x+h_2 x^2+..., the equation 2 H' = 1+H^2 determines h_{m+1} recursively from h_0,...,h_m by comparing coefficients of x^m. Hence the solution with constant term 1 is unique, so F(x)=G(x)=sec x + tan x.

Also, by the Cauchy product,
sum_{n>=1} W_n(z) x^{n-1}/(n-1)! = F(zx) F(x).

Since S_odd = S_even, we have W_n(-1)=0 for every n>=2, so W_n(z) is divisible by 1+z. Write W_n(z)=(1+z) Q_n(z).

Next we show that Q_n has strictly positive coefficients. Using F(t)=tan(pi/4+t/2), let A=pi/4+u/2 and B=pi/4+v/2. Then
(F(u)F(v)-1)/(F(u)+F(v)) = (tan A tan B - 1)/(tan A + tan B) = -cot(A+B) = tan((u+v)/2).
So
F(u)F(v)-1 = tan((u+v)/2) (F(u)+F(v)).
With u=zx and v=x this becomes
sum_{n>=2} Q_n(z) x^{n-1}/(n-1)! = [tan((1+z)x/2)/(1+z)] * (F(zx)+F(x)).

Now tan t = sum_{m>=0} E_{2m+1} t^{2m+1}/(2m+1)!, because F(t)-F(-t)=2 tan t and the odd coefficients of F are exactly E_{2m+1}. Hence
 tan((1+z)x/2)/(1+z) = sum_{m>=0} E_{2m+1} (1+z)^{2m} x^{2m+1} / ((2m+1)! 2^{2m+1}),
which has nonnegative coefficients in x and z. The series
 F(zx)+F(x) = sum_{r>=0} E_r (z^r+1) x^r/r!
also has nonnegative coefficients. Therefore every polynomial Q_n(z) has nonnegative coefficients.

In fact those coefficients are all positive. If n is even, then in the product above the constant term 2 from F(zx)+F(x) multiplied by the x^{n-1} term of tan((1+z)x/2)/(1+z) contributes a positive multiple of (1+z)^{n-2} x^{n-1}; hence every coefficient of Q_n is positive. If n is odd, the x-term (1+z)x from F(zx)+F(x) multiplied by the x^{n-2} term of tan((1+z)x/2)/(1+z) contributes a positive multiple of (1+z)^{n-2} x^{n-1}; again every coefficient of Q_n is positive.

So write Q_n(z)=q_1+q_2 z+...+q_{n-1} z^{n-2} with q_i>0. Because W_n(z)=(1+z)Q_n(z), if we set q_0=q_n=0 then
w_j = q_{j-1}+q_j for every 1<=j<=n.

Now let P be any subset of {1,...,n} with no two consecutive elements. Then
sum_{j in P} w_j = sum_{j in P} (q_{j-1}+q_j)
= sum_{i=1}^{n-1} q_i (1_{i in P} + 1_{i+1 in P}).
Since P has no consecutive integers, for each i at most one of i and i+1 lies in P, so 1_{i in P} + 1_{i+1 in P} <= 1. Therefore
sum_{j in P} w_j <= sum_{i=1}^{n-1} q_i = Q_n(1) = W_n(1)/2 = (S_odd+S_even)/2 = E_n.
But E_n = S_odd = S_even, so
sum_{j in P} w_j <= max(S_odd,S_even).
This proves the first assertion.

For the equality statement, the extra hypothesis S_odd = S_even is automatic from the first part. Because every q_i is strictly positive, equality in the displayed inequality holds exactly when 1_{i in P} + 1_{i+1 in P} = 1 for every i=1,...,n-1; that is, every adjacent pair {i,i+1} contains exactly one element of P. On a path this forces P to be one of the two parity classes: if 1 is in P, then 2 is not, then 3 is, and so on, so P is exactly the odd-index set; if 1 is not in P, then 2 is, then 3 is not, etc., so P is exactly the even-index set. Conversely those two sets have weights S_odd and S_even respectively, hence they do attain equality.

Therefore the lemma is proved.
solver_summary: Interpret w_j combinatorially: for odd j it counts alternating permutations with 1 in position j, and for even j it counts alternating permutations with n in position j. This gives S_odd=S_even=E_n and the convolution recurrence 2E_{m+1}=sum_k binom(m,k)E_kE_{m-k}. From this, the exponential generating function F(x)=sum E_r x^r/r! satisfies 2F'=1+F^2, hence F=sec x+tan x. For W_n(z)=sum_j w_j z^{j-1}, one has sum_n W_n(z)x^{n-1}/(n-1)!=F(zx)F(x). Using the identity F(u)F(v)-1=tan((u+v)/2)(F(u)+F(v)), we get W_n(z)=(1+z)Q_n(z) where Q_n has strictly positive coefficients. Writing Q_n(z)=sum_{i=1}^{n-1} q_i z^{i-1}, this means w_j=q_{j-1}+q_j with all q_i>0. For any P with no consecutive indices, each q_i can be counted by at most one of the adjacent vertices i and i+1, so sum_{j in P}w_j<=sum_i q_i=E_n=S_odd=S_even=max(S_odd,S_even). Equality requires every q_i to be counted exactly once, i.e. every adjacent pair contains exactly one chosen vertex, which forces P to be exactly the odd set or exactly the even set.
vetter_reason: The proof strategy is on target and the main combinatorial/generating-function argument appears mathematically sound, but there is a localized indexing gap in the transition to the differential equation. The proof establishes S_odd = S_even = E_n only for n >= 2, not for n = 1, so the derived recurrence 2 E_{m+1} = sum_{k=0}^m binom(m,k) E_k E_{m-k} is justified only for m >= 1. The step 'Therefore 2 F'(x) = 1 + F(x)^2' needs an explicit separate check of the constant term m = 0. With that repair, the rest of the proof supports the lemma.
